issue.issue_text: Whether the circumstance of 'last seen', based on the testimonies of PW-8 and PW-10, was sufficiently proven by the prosecution to form a conclusive chain of circumstantial evidence against the accused.

facts: The prosecution's case against the accused was based entirely on circumstantial evidence.
A crucial circumstance relied upon by the prosecution was the 'last seen' theory, which was based on the oral testimonies of two witnesses, PW-8 and PW-10.
The Trial Court and the High Court had both accepted these testimonies and held that the 'last seen' circumstance was proven.
law: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the proof of an important circumstance like 'last seen' depends on the quality, nature, and reliability of the witness testimonies.
For such a circumstance to be established, the evidence must be conclusive and form a complete chain that unerringly points to the guilt of the accused.
application: The Supreme Court conducted its own "careful scrutiny" of the evidence provided by PW-8 and PW-10.
The Court found that the lower courts had failed to properly consider whether the testimony of PW-10 actually corroborated the testimony of PW-8.
Upon review, the Court determined that the testimonies of PW-8 and PW-10 were "at variance" with each other and therefore "inconclusive."
The Court held that the evidence of PW-10 not only failed to support PW-8's account but actually cast it "under a shadow of doubt."
Furthermore, the Court found it "unsafe" to rely on the sole testimony of PW-8, especially since he only had a "nodding acquaintance" with the accused.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the lower courts' finding, concluding that the prosecution had failed to sufficiently prove the 'last seen' circumstance. The testimonies of PW-8 and PW-10 were contradictory and doubtful, making the evidence inconclusive and breaking a critical link in the chain of circumstantial evidence against the accused.

cases.principle: The Supreme Court can interfere with concurrent findings of lower courts under Article 136 of the Constitution if the evidence has been improperly appreciated, material aspects have been ignored, or the findings are perverse. In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances must be fully proved, be of a conclusive nature pointing to the guilt of the accused, and form an unbroken chain.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court will interfere with the concurrent findings of lower courts under Article 136 of the Constitution where the evidence has not been properly appreciated, material aspects have been ignored, or the findings are perverse. In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must establish that the circumstances are fully proved, conclusive in nature, consistent only with the hypothesis of guilt, and form a complete chain that excludes the possibility of guilt of any person other than the accused.
obiter: The law laid down relating circumstantial evidence in those decisions are unfailingly followed by this Court while dealing with the cases where conviction is rested on circumstantial evidence.

The law relating to circumstantial evidence no longer remains res integra and it has been held by catena of decisions of this Court that the circumstances proved should lead to no other inference except that of the guilt of the accused so that, the accused can be convicted of the offences charged.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When the above being the factual position obtained from the oral testimonies of PW-8 and PW-10, the Hon’ble High Court which observed that the circumstance of ‘last seen’ is an important circumstance in the case on hand and its proof would depend upon the quality and nature of the testimonies of PW-8 and PW-10 should have bestowed a threadbare, serious consideration to answer the question whether the circumstance was proved by the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt.
legal_tests_applied: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances from which an inference of guilt is sought to be drawn should be fully proved and such circumstances must be of a conclusive nature pointing to the guilt of the accused. There shall be no gap in such chain of circumstances.

The circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency, unerringly point to the guilt of the accused and further, all the circumstances taken together are incapable of any explanation on any reasonable hypothesis save the guilt of the accused.
The failure to establish an alleged motive in a case based on circumstantial evidence weakens the case of the prosecution.
why_respondent_won: The evidence regarding the 'last seen' theory was inconclusive due to variance in the testimonies.
The High Court failed to conduct a 'threadbare, serious consideration' of the testimonies of the 'last seen' witnesses, PW-8 and PW-10, to properly assess if the circumstance was proven.
The prosecution miserably failed to prove the alleged motive, which is a factor that weakens the case and weighs in favour of the accused in a circumstantial evidence case.
Other circumstantial evidence, such as the recovery of a weapon and dress, was not conclusive as the panch witnesses for the recovery did not support the prosecution.

The cumulative effect of the weak links in the chain of evidence, including the inconclusive 'last seen' theory and the failure to prove motive, meant that the circumstances did not unerringly point to the guilt of the appellants.
policy_considerations: Where the evidence has not been properly appreciated, material aspects have been ignored and the findings are perverse, the Supreme Court will interfere with the concurrent findings of the courts below to prevent a miscarriage of justice.

When the circumstantial evidence presented is not sufficient to form a conclusive chain that unerringly points to guilt, it is unsafe to maintain a conviction, and the benefit of the doubt must be extended to the accused.
